stories.headline: Walmart sales crawl at a six-year low as $4 gas makes shoppers pick cabbage or gas
stories.dek: US same-store sales rose only 2.6%. Shares fell about 9%. A $2.9 billion tariff refund will fund price cuts.
stories.caveman: Walmart is the giant US shop. If poor and middle people stop buying, Walmart feels it first. For the quarter that ended July 31, sales in US stores open at least a year grew only 2.6 percent. That is the slowest since the first pandemic months in 2020. Wall Street wanted more. The stock dropped about 8 to 9 percent Thursday and dragged the whole market down. Bosses say gas over 4 dollars a gallon makes people trade off. AAA had gas near 4.10 dollars. Walmart still made a fat profit, about 6.4 billion dollars, because online sales jumped 24 percent and because the Supreme Court said Trump's big import taxes were illegal. The government owed Walmart a 2.9 billion dollar tariff refund, the biggest yet. Walmart says it will use that money to cut prices on 11,000 things. It also expects about 2 billion extra dollars in fuel costs this year because of the Iran war.
stories.why_it_matters: Walmart is a thermometer for regular US wallets. If the cheapest shop is slow, the squeeze from war oil is already in the grocery aisle, not just at the pump.
stories.camps: Walmart says it is still stealing shoppers, especially richer ones, and that refunds will pay for cheaper shelves. Investors punished the slow stores and the careful outlook. Workers and low-income shoppers eat the gas bill either way. Trump wanted tariffs as a trophy; the Court made companies send the trophy money back, and now shops race to look like the hero of lower prices.

terms.explain: Sales in shops that were already open last year, so new stores do not fake the growth.
Money customs gives back after a court says an import tax was illegal.
A tax on stuff coming in from another country.

stories.image_alt: Walmart store sign against a blue sky

stories.headline: The Treasury's bond-buy hug lasted one day. Yields jumped back and stocks fell
stories.dek: Reuters: Dow off about 1.3 percent, S&P 500 about 0.9 percent. The 30-year yield returned to 5.24 percent.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday the US Treasury said it would buy back twice as much long-term government paper, at least 4 billion dollars a pop, to calm a jumpy bond market. Yields, the interest the government pays, dipped. Thursday they climbed again. The 30-year yield went to about 5.24 percent, up from 5.19, still under Tuesday's 5.33 peak. The 10-year sat near 4.70 percent. US stocks fell to a two-week low. Reuters put the Dow down about 1.3 percent, the S&P 500 down about 0.9 percent, the Nasdaq down about 1 percent. Walmart's miss, down about 9 percent, and another oil jump added weight. Nine of eleven S&P sectors fell. One bright oddity: a sale of 30-year inflation-protected bonds drew the strongest demand since December 2020. Bitcoin rose about 5 percent and crossed 70,000 dollars. Next week money bosses gather at Jackson Hole.
stories.why_it_matters: If long-term yields stay high, mortgages and company loans stay expensive. A one-day Treasury hug does not fix a mountain of new borrowing plus war oil.
stories.camps: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says this is plumbing, not a rescue. Skeptics say the government is buying its own IOUs because private buyers got picky. Incoming Fed talk and oil keep the hawks loud.

terms.explain: The interest a bond pays. When yields jump, new borrowing gets pricier.
The government buys its own old IOUs so fewer sit in the market.
A yearly Fed camp in Wyoming where money bosses hint what they will do next.

stories.image_alt: Traders in blue jackets on the New York Stock Exchange floor

stories.headline: Brent oil jumped toward 94 dollars after Trump promised an economic D-Day on Iran
stories.dek: Thursday close: Brent about 93.78 dollars, up 2.4 percent. Hormuz is still a choke point.
stories.caveman: Brent is the world's main oil price sticker. On Thursday it rose about 2.4 percent to about 93.78 dollars a barrel. US oil, WTI, rose to about 87.83. That is a four-week high and part of a two-week climb of about 20 percent. The spark was Trump's Wednesday-night post promising economic war on Iran and on any country that still feeds it money. Hormuz, the skinny sea door for about a fifth of seaborne oil, is still a mess. JPMorgan says each extra month of disruption can add about 7 to 8 dollars a barrel. If it lasts three months they see monthly averages near 114. Goldman Sachs has warned Brent could hit 120 if the strait stays clogged, while their calmer guess is 80 in the fourth quarter. Traders are not waiting for the calm guess.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil in the 90s leaks into diesel, food trucks, and then into the Fed's next fight. Taiwan pays it in shipping and in the cost of stuff on boats.
stories.camps: Hawks say squeeze Iran until Hormuz opens. Iran says the squeeze is economic terrorism and the strait stays a weapon. Banks print scary numbers and calmer numbers in the same note. Drivers just see the pump.

terms.explain: The main world oil price, named after a North Sea field.
The main US oil price sticker.
A skinny sea door by Iran. A lot of the world's oil boats go through it.

stories.image_alt: Oil market or tanker image from coverage of the Iran-driven price jump

stories.headline: US government debt crossed 40 trillion dollars, faster than the official guess
stories.dek: Treasury books showed 40.047 trillion on Tuesday. It took less than five months to climb from 39 trillion.
stories.caveman: The US government now owes a little over 40 trillion dollars. That is the gross pile: about 32.3 trillion in bonds the public holds, plus about 7.8 trillion the government owes its own pots like Social Security. Treasury published the number Wednesday. Watchdogs noted it took less than five months to go from 39 trillion to 40. In January 2017 the whole pile was under 20 trillion. PBS, walking through the books Thursday, said interest on the debt is already bigger than what Washington spends on the military or on Medicare. The IMF's tracker puts US debt at about 126 percent of one year's national output. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said America can grow its way out. Budget hawks say that is a wish, not a plan.
stories.why_it_matters: A country that borrows this much pays more just to stand still. That leaks into your mortgage, your taxes, and how much money is left for hospitals and schools.
stories.camps: Bessent says grow out of it. Deficit hawks want tax rises or spending cuts or both. Many left critics say tax cuts for the rich and forever wars did this, not school lunches. Trump talks tough on waste while the pile grows on his watch too.

terms.explain: All the money the US government owes, including IOUs to itself.
Money one US government pocket owes another, like borrowing from Social Security.
How big the debt is compared with one year of the country's output.

stories.image_alt: US Treasury or debt visual from coverage of the 40 trillion milestone

stories.headline: Google lets you mash a 'favorite source' button so AI Search might send you back to real sites
stories.dek: Thursday: publishers can embed Preferred Sources. Google says favorites get twice the clicks. Traffic is still dying.
stories.caveman: Google's robot answers now eat the clicks that used to pay newspapers. On Thursday Google gave publishers a little bone. Sites can put a button on their own pages. You press it to say this site is a favorite. Google promises to show that site more in Search, Discover, and Google News, and in its AI answer boxes. The company first put Preferred Sources into Top Stories, then into AI Mode and AI Overviews in May. It says people had already picked more than 345,000 different sources. Old tests said people were twice as likely to click a favorite. Google will also let you talk to your Discover feed in plain words, like 'less celebrity, more labor', and let Android users tune the spoken news briefing. Publishers have heard nice Google promises before.
stories.why_it_matters: If AI answers keep the reader inside Google, reporters do not get paid. A button is not a law. It is a sales pitch while the floor keeps dropping.
stories.camps: Google says this is how trust works now: you pick the humans you believe. Publishers say they need money, not a widget. Readers just want fewer junk answers.

terms.explain: Google's list of websites you say you trust, so those links show up more.
Google's robot summary at the top of search. Often people stop there and never click.
Google's phone feed of stories it thinks you want.

stories.image_alt: Google Preferred Sources button shown in product images

stories.headline: ChatGPT on a Mac can now read and send your iMessages
stories.dek: OpenAI shipped an Apple Messages plug-in Thursday. It runs on Apple silicon only. You are supposed to approve each send.
stories.caveman: OpenAI put a plug-in in the ChatGPT desktop app for Mac. It can open Apple Messages, search old chats, draft a reply, delete a text, and send iMessage, SMS, or RCS as you. It works inside Codex and ChatGPT Work, the agent desks, not in a normal chatbot window. It is only for Apple silicon Macs, not old Intel ones, and not on the phone. OpenAI told Bloomberg the plug-in runs on your machine and does not build a giant index of every text. The default is: you look at the message and the names, then you say yes. OpenAI warns that turning on 'always allow' means the robot can send as you with no last look. Privacy people already smell a rat. A robot with your whole text history is a gift to scammers if the lock slips.
stories.why_it_matters: Your texts are the last private diary a lot of people have. Handing the diary to a company racing toward an IPO is a big trust jump, even if they swear the diary stays on the laptop.
stories.camps: OpenAI says local plus approve-before-send is safe enough. Privacy advocates want a hard no on always-allow and a clearer map of what leaves the Mac. Apple has not made this a system feature, so OpenAI is bolting it on.

terms.explain: A small add-on that lets one program drive another program.
Macs with Apple's own chips, not old Intel chips.
OpenAI's agent desks that can do longer jobs, not just chat.

stories.image_alt: ChatGPT or smartphone messaging visual from the plug-in coverage
stories.image_credit: Photo: Gabby Jones / Bloomberg / Getty Images

stories.headline: Alation, an AI data shop sitting inside half the Fortune 1000, says it got hacked
stories.dek: Thursday confirmation after a Tuesday outage. The company will not say if files walked out.
stories.caveman: Alation sells software that lets big companies ask their own messy files questions in plain words. It says it serves more than 500 firms, including about half of the Fortune 1000, the biggest US companies. On Tuesday some customers saw the system wobble for about an hour. On Thursday Alation told TechCrunch there was 'unauthorized activity in one of its systems' and that it is investigating. It would not say how many customers got hit, whether data was stolen, or what those customers should do. A lot of its computers live on Amazon's cloud. This fits a grim pattern: hackers go after the companies that hold other companies' secrets, because one break opens many safes.
stories.why_it_matters: If the catalog of a company's private data is cracked, the thief does not need to rob each office. One key, many doors.
stories.camps: Alation calls it isolated and still investigating. Customers want a straight answer on stolen files. Security reporters note the company has not even said whether it warned the people who pay it.

terms.explain: A US company that sells data catalogs and AI search over a firm's own files.
The 1,000 biggest US companies by revenue.
Someone breaking into computers without permission.

stories.image_alt: Alation company logo from the cyberattack report

stories.headline: US agencies say hackers are using AI to break the little computers that run water plants
stories.dek: CISA, FBI, and NSA: all Siemens S7 controllers are in the crosshairs. Towns in five states already reported hits.
stories.caveman: Water plants and factories use small tough computers called programmable logic controllers to open valves and run pumps. Many US ones are old Siemens S7 boxes. On Wednesday, CISA, the FBI, and the NSA warned that hackers are going after all of those boxes. The agencies say the attackers use AI to write break-in scripts from public manuals, then hit machines that are old, online, or badly locked. A hit can stop water, wreck gear, or cause a safety accident. Officials have seen break-ins at water sites in Minnesota, Michigan, Arkansas, Georgia, and New Jersey. CISA has long said these boxes should not face the open internet. Rural towns get hit harder because one plant covers a lot of land. The warning sits on top of months of suspected Iranian probing of US water systems.
stories.why_it_matters: You do not need a missile to make a town thirsty. An old pump computer on the internet is enough, and AI makes the hunting cheap.
stories.camps: Agencies say patch, disconnect, and watch. An incident responder told TechCrunch the AI angle is newsworthy but the boxes were already soft. Cities want money for upgrades. Vendors sold the boxes decades ago and moved on.

terms.explain: The US civilian cyber-defense agency.
A small industrial computer that runs pumps, valves, and factory lines.
The systems a country needs to live: water, power, food, hospitals.

stories.image_alt: Water treatment infrastructure from the CISA warning coverage
stories.image_credit: Photo: Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times

stories.headline: Ukraine's parliament made spy-general Yevhenii Khmara the new defense minister
stories.dek: Lawmakers voted 312 to 2 on Wednesday. Zelensky wants more long-range strikes. The ousted minister wants elections.
stories.caveman: Ukraine's parliament, the Rada, confirmed Yevhenii Khmara as defense minister on Wednesday, 312 votes to 2. You only needed 226. Khmara is a career officer from the SBU, the security service. He used to run Alpha, a special unit tied in reports to Operation Spiderweb, last year's deep drone hits inside Russia. The law says the defense minister must be a civilian, so he dropped his general rank to take the job. He is the fifth defense minister since Russia's full-scale invasion. President Zelensky told him to grow long-range strikes, thicken air defense, and fix how the army buys gear. The last minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, was pushed out in July after a public fight with the army chief. On Tuesday Fedorov posted a video saying Ukraine has a system crisis and should move toward elections, which wartime law now blocks. Dozens protested in Kyiv on Wednesday. Some want a vote. Many doubt you can hold one while missiles fall.
stories.why_it_matters: A country at war just changed the person who buys the missiles, while the last boss asked a forbidden question: who gets to choose the government if the war lasts years?
stories.camps: Zelensky says Ukraine needs more strength. Khmara promises to shrink Russia's war machine. Fedorov and street protesters say the system is rotting without a vote. Russia is happy to watch Kyiv fight itself.

terms.explain: Ukraine's new defense minister. Came from the SBU spy service.
Ukraine's main security and intelligence service.
Emergency war rules. In Ukraine they pause elections.

stories.image_alt: Yevhenii Khmara in uniform speaking at a podium with Ukraine and EU flags

stories.headline: Russia killed at least 18 people in Ukraine on Thursday as Patriot missiles run thin
stories.dek: Air force: 44 missiles, 39 shot down. A nine-story building collapsed in Kyiv. Poland and Romania scrambled jets.
stories.caveman: Thursday was another beating. Ukraine says Russia fired at least 44 missiles and a wave of jet-powered drones. The air force said it shot down 39 missiles. At least 18 people died, most in Kyiv. A nine-story apartment house in the Solomianskyi district fell and burned. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a children's hospital nearby lost windows. People were trapped in rubble. Power went out in parts of two districts. An overnight attack lasted about nine hours and also hit warehouses in Boryspil. Russia said it struck military factories and logistics. Neighbors got nervous. Poland put planes and air defenses up along the border. Romania said a drone crossed near Galati and crashed in empty land in Tulcea. Reporters in Kyiv said the scary part is the cupboard: Ukraine is short of Patriot interceptor missiles, the expensive arrows that kill ballistic missiles. Winter energy plants will be next if the cupboard stays empty.
stories.why_it_matters: When interceptors run out, apartments become the shield. NATO's edge states already scramble as if the war is leaking.
stories.camps: Kyiv begs partners for more Patriots. Washington is busy in the Gulf. Moscow wants the lights off before winter. Families in Solomianskyi just want the building to stop falling.

terms.explain: A US-made missile that tries to kill incoming missiles. Ukraine does not have enough.
A fast rocket that goes high and comes down hard. Harder to shoot than a slow drone.

stories.image_alt: Aftermath or air-alert coverage from Thursday's strikes on Kyiv

stories.headline: Trump declared an 'economic D-Day' on Iran and on any country still feeding it
stories.dek: Wednesday-night Truth Social blast. No list of targets. UAE already cut ties. China said sanctions will not settle it.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday evening Trump wrote in all caps that he was launching 'economic D-Day' on Iran, 'the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country.' He said any country whose banks, shops, airports, or ministries give Iran a lifeline will face 'tremendous' economic pain. He named oil smuggling, swap lines, cash shops, ship flags, and front companies. He did not name the countries. A 60-day ceasefire had died on Monday. The US-Israel war on Iran is about six months old. On Tuesday the UAE, a US ally that used to be a huge door for Iran money, said it was freezing all trade and finance with Tehran after it tracked two Iranian ballistic missiles toward sea traffic. China's embassy in Washington told the BBC that sanctions and pressure do not fix this. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, called the post a diversion from America's own money problems and 'economic terrorism.' Details of the new punishments were still thin Thursday.
stories.why_it_matters: If Washington really punches every bank that still touches Iran, China, Gulf traders, and oil prices all get hit. If it is just shouting, markets still jump and civilians still pay.
stories.camps: Trump wants a win before November votes and cheaper gas, which this threat does not instantly deliver. Iran says the strait is its lever. China wants to keep buying cheap barrels. Gulf states are picking sides under missile threat.

terms.explain: Trump's name for a bigger money war on Iran, including punishing other countries that still deal with it.
Punishing someone else's bank or buyer for dealing with the first target.
A Gulf country. Dubai was a big door for Iran money. It said it shut that door this week.

stories.image_alt: Donald Trump in coverage of the economic D-Day announcement

stories.headline: Taiwan asked for a record 35 billion dollar defense budget as China keeps circling
stories.dek: 1.12 trillion Taiwan dollars for 2027, over 3 percent of GDP, an 18 percent jump. The opposition legislature still has to pass it.
stories.caveman: Taiwan's government on Thursday proposed spending 1.12 trillion Taiwan dollars, about 35 billion US dollars, on defense next year. That is the first time the yearly defense budget would clear one trillion, an 18 percent jump, and more than 3 percent of the island's output. President Lai Ching-te has promised 5 percent by 2030. The US has been nagging Taipei to spend more. The same US president, after a May sit-down with Xi Jinping, called arms sales to Taiwan 'a very good negotiating chip' with Beijing, which scared people on the island. Xi had warned that a clumsy Taiwan policy could mean a clash. The plan now goes to an opposition-controlled legislature that only passed this year's national budget last Friday, after a 266-day stall. China still flies planes and sails ships around Taiwan and has not given up the threat of force.
stories.why_it_matters: Money on paper is not missiles in sheds. If Washington treats Taiwan weapons as a bargain chip, Beijing hears a wobble.
stories.camps: Lai says defense spending is peace spending. The opposition can trim the bill. Washington wants Taiwan to pay more and also wants a deal with Xi. Beijing calls the whole budget a separatist show.

terms.explain: Taiwan's president. He wants defense spending at 5 percent of GDP by 2030.
The size of an economy in one year. Defense as a share of GDP is how people compare military effort.

stories.image_alt: Taiwan military aircraft in file coverage of the defense budget

stories.headline: Richard Russo's new small-town novel jumped straight onto the indie fiction list
stories.dek: Under the Falls debuts at No. 7 on the Aug. 19 IndieBound list, week ending Aug. 16. Knopf, 256 pages.
stories.caveman: Richard Russo won a Pulitzer for Empire Falls, a sad-funny book about a dying mill town. His new one, Under the Falls, landed in US independent bookstores and debuted at No. 7 on the national hardcover fiction list that IndieBound published Wednesday. The book came out Aug. 11 from Knopf. It is short, about 256 pages, 30 dollars. A musician named Tyler Sinclair left Stone Mountain at 18. Eighteen years later he comes back with his band for a benefit gig and finds the past has teeth. Indie booksellers like Russo because he still writes about leftover America, not just Brooklyn parties. A debut at 7 in a week full of giant names means the old guy still sells when the shipment hits the table.
stories.why_it_matters: Indie lists tell you what people buy when Amazon is not whispering. A Pulitzer novelist opening at 7 is a signal that brick stores still have a house author.
stories.camps: Russo fans wanted another trip to broken towns. Thriller readers get a crime plot. People who only read new debuts may skip it. Bookstores put it face-out anyway.

terms.explain: American novelist. Pulitzer for Empire Falls. Writes small-town US life.
The bestseller list from independent US bookstores, not Amazon.
A major US literary publisher, part of Penguin Random House.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Under the Falls by Richard Russo

stories.headline: Who's hot: Riley Sager and dungeon nerds. Who's not: Whitehead slipped
stories.dek: New IndieBound week: The Unknown climbs to 6. Cool Machine falls 6 to 9. Matt Dinniman keeps eating the list.
stories.caveman: US indie shops posted a new national list Wednesday for the week ending Aug. 16. Caro Claire Burke's tradwife nightmare Yesteryear is still No. 1, week 19, so that story is old. The move is lower down. Riley Sager's island-disappearance thriller The Unknown climbed from 7 to 6 in only its second week. Colson Whitehead's Cool Machine, Harlem in the 1980s, dropped from 6 to 9 after four weeks. That is not a crash, but it is a cooling. Meanwhile Matt Dinniman's goofy-bloody Dungeon Crawler Carl world keeps multiplying: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook rose 10 to 8, The Gate of the Feral Gods 12 to 11, and the paperbacks still squat in the top five. Robert Jackson Bennett's A Trade of Blood tumbled 8 to 14. Ann Patchett's Whistler holds at 2. The list is a fight between literary names and people who want a cat named Princess Donut to punch a god.
stories.why_it_matters: A list is a weather report. Thrillers and LitRPG are taking table space from prize-winning literary fiction this week.
stories.camps: Literary readers shrug and wait. Genre readers are eating the store. Booksellers need both: Patchett for the regulars, Dinniman for the kids who found Carl on a phone.

terms.explain: US thriller writer. New book The Unknown is climbing indie lists.
Stories where life is a video-game dungeon. Matt Dinniman's Carl books are the current craze.
American novelist. Two Pulitzers. Cool Machine is book three of his Harlem trilogy.

stories.image_alt: Cover of The Unknown by Riley Sager, climbing the indie list

stories.headline: Chris Smalls takes his Amazon-union memoir to Harlem this weekend
stories.dek: When the Revolution Comes is a Penguin Random House memoir. Event Saturday on Malcolm X Boulevard.
stories.caveman: Chris Smalls helped win the first Amazon warehouse union vote in the US, at Staten Island's JFK8 in 2022, after Amazon fired him for a 2020 COVID walkout. His memoir, When the Revolution Comes: A Fight for the Future of the Working Class, is out from Penguin Random House. He told the Amsterdam News it took about four years, three writing and one making the book. It starts in a warehouse, then jumps back to childhood, odd jobs, marriage, kids, getting fired, then organizing. He no longer holds a union title and says he does not want one. He has been taking the book, and the organizing, through more than 45 countries. Saturday Aug. 22 he is due at a Grassroots of Harlem citizenry book party at 369 Malcolm X Boulevard. US union membership was about 10 percent in 2025, and only about 5.9 percent in the private sector. Smalls wants more Black and Brown workers in labor leadership, not just on the floor.
stories.why_it_matters: Amazon tried to make the warehouse a story about one loud man. The book tries to make it a story about a class. Harlem is where he is planting that this week.
stories.camps: Labor people treat Smalls as proof a warehouse can vote yes. Amazon still fights unions. Some union old guard bristle at a leader with no title. Readers get a memoir, not a manual.

terms.explain: US labor organizer. Helped win the Amazon Labor Union vote at JFK8 in 2022.
The union that won a vote at Amazon's Staten Island warehouse.
A book someone writes about their own life.

stories.image_alt: Cover of When the Revolution Comes by Chris Smalls
stories.image_credit: Cover: Penguin Random House / Amsterdam News

stories.headline: Emily Wilson's Odyssey leaped to No. 3 paperback as the Nolan movie heat hits shops
stories.dek: IndieBound: 7 to 3 this week. The US translator's Homer is the edition stores are stacking for the film.
stories.caveman: Emily Wilson, a US classicist, made a plain-English Odyssey in 2018 that a lot of teachers actually like. Independent US shops just moved that paperback from No. 7 to No. 3 on the national list. IndieBound's own blurb now calls it inspiration for Christopher Nolan's big-screen Homer. Wilson's line is famous for starting with 'Tell me about a complicated man' instead of dusty 'muse' talk. When a movie of an old poem is coming, stores do not always stock the old Victorian version. They stock the one people can read on the subway. Circe by Madeline Miller, another Greek-myth hit, sits nearby at 7. This is how classics survive in the US: a living translator plus a Hollywood engine, then a stack by the register.
stories.why_it_matters: A 3,000-year-old poem is a bestseller again because a woman in Pennsylvania made the sentences walk, and a famous director pointed a camera at the story.
stories.camps: Classicists argue about every word. Movie people want a hero. Booksellers just want the edition that rings. Wilson's fans say the older boy-club translations can sit down.

terms.explain: US scholar and translator. Her Odyssey is the one US indies are selling hard this week.
An ancient Greek poem about a soldier trying to get home. Many English versions exist.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Emily Wilson's translation of The Odyssey

stories.headline: UN: 94 percent of Gaza needs shelter, and Israel still blocks the tents
stories.dek: About 1.98 million people. Four in five families live in critical or catastrophic conditions. Fifty old dead, 19 of them children, were buried Thursday.
stories.caveman: On Thursday UN agencies said 94 percent of Gaza's 2.1 million people need shelter and basic household stuff. The Shelter Cluster, led by the Norwegian Refugee Council, put the count near 1.98 million. More than four in five families now live in what aid people call critical or catastrophic conditions: not enough fuel, light, water storage, or a roof that can take rain. Nearly two-thirds live in tents meant for a few weeks, not another winter. Last winter more than 70 percent of families got flooded. Partners say they need about 562 million dollars, and Israel still restricts tents, repair gear, fuel, and heavy machines. Thursday, Gaza buried 50 people, including 19 children, whose bodies had just been pulled from rubble. They had been dead about two years. The World Food Programme still reaches about 1.5 million people with food. Pest teams have hit more than 3,250 dirty sites because rats live in the ruins.
stories.why_it_matters: A ceasefire rumor does not make a tent a house. If winter comes with the same blockade, the next flood is already scheduled.
stories.camps: Israel says security. The UN says civilians are being squeezed past dignity. Donors underfund the appeal. Families sleep in plastic and wait for machines that do not arrive.

terms.explain: The aid group that coordinates tents, tarps, and household kits in a crisis. In Gaza it is led by the Norwegian Refugee Council.
The UN office that coordinates emergency aid.

stories.image_alt: Collapsed apartment block in Gaza with a Qatar Fund tent in the rubble

stories.headline: Congo gets 70,000 Ebola shots as a Bundibugyo outbreak becomes the deadliest on its books
stories.dek: WHO: 5,021 cases, 2,325 dead. The vaccine was built for a different strain. War with M23 is blocking the nurses.
stories.caveman: The Democratic Republic of the Congo will get 70,000 doses of Ervebo, an Ebola vaccine, from the global emergency stockpile. WHO said Thursday that 50,000 doses go to health workers and 20,000 go into a clinical trial. The catch: Ervebo was built for Zaire ebolavirus, the West Africa killer, not the Bundibugyo strain now spreading. Lab and animal hints say it might help. Nobody knows until people get it. The outbreak was declared May 15. By Wednesday there were 5,021 cases and 2,325 deaths, the country's deadliest Ebola wave on record. More than 160 health workers caught it and 40 died. War in the east, the government versus Rwanda-backed M23 and other armed groups, blocks tracing, safe burials, and clinic access. M23 even claims it is running its own Ebola shops and said Thursday it would stop shared taxis and boats from government zones. The UN has sanctioned M23 for atrocities. Vaccines on a tarmac do not walk through a front line.
stories.why_it_matters: A virus plus a war is how outbreaks become graveyards. Health workers are already dying in double digits.
stories.camps: WHO calls the shipment solidarity. Scientists say the trial is the honest part, because the shot might not fit this strain. M23 wants to look like a state. Patients just need a nurse who can reach them.

terms.explain: A deadly virus. Ervebo is a vaccine made for one strain. Bundibugyo is a different strain now in Congo.
A Rwanda-backed armed group fighting the Congo government in the east.
The international group that unlocks emergency vaccine stockpiles in outbreaks.

stories.headline: Lebanon: 860,000 went home to wreckage, and Israeli strikes still push people north
stories.dek: 360,000 remain displaced. UNIFIL counted 9 airstrikes and 265 projectiles Monday to Wednesday. The flash appeal is half empty.
stories.caveman: The UN says about 860,000 people displaced by the south Lebanon war have gone back toward home. That sounds like the end. It is not. About 360,000 are still displaced, including at least 22,000 in collective shelters. Many returnees cannot enter smashed houses. They rent, crowd in with family, or camp nearby. More than 700,000 people still live with broken water systems. The big UN flash appeal, 639.9 million dollars, is only 48 percent funded. UNHCR's own Lebanon budget is 24 percent funded. A US-brokered ceasefire in late June said Hezbollah disarms and Israel leaves the south. Fighting never fully stopped. UN peacekeepers, UNIFIL, told the UN Thursday that from Monday to Wednesday they saw 86 airspace violations, 9 Israeli airstrikes, 265 projectiles, and almost 30 drone events, plus demolitions and blocked patrols. Weekend strikes already sent hundreds of families fleeing north again.
stories.why_it_matters: Going home to a house with no water is not recovery. A half-funded appeal plus new bombs means the next displacement wave is already walking.
stories.camps: Israel says it is hitting Hezbollah. The UN says civilians, water pipes, and peacekeepers are in the way. Lebanon's government has a return plan on paper. Donors have not paid for the pipes.

stories.headline: In Haiti, cutting USAID did what gangs wanted: more hungry kids to recruit
stories.dek: New Humanitarian, Aug. 19: child recruitment tripled in 2025. 1.5 million displaced. Gangs hold about 90 percent of Port-au-Prince.
stories.caveman: Haiti's capital is mostly run by armed groups. They hold about 90 percent of Port-au-Prince. A record 1.5 million people are displaced. UNICEF says the number of children pulled into gangs tripled in 2025, and kids now make up about half of gang members. The New Humanitarian reported Wednesday that Trump's 2025 freeze and the gutting of USAID wiped out a lot of the boring programs that kept teenagers busy: bike repair, haircutting, seedling jobs worth about 4 dollars a day. The US used to cover more than 65 percent of humanitarian aid in Haiti. OCHA said the freeze halted about 80 percent of US-funded programs. About 6.4 million people, of nearly 12 million, still need help. UNICEF's Haiti appeal was 79 percent unfunded at mid-year. Washington still spends on a Gang Suppression Force. Peace groups that used to run trauma talks have closed offices. A 14-year-old told reporters he killed four people after a gang fed him twice a day. 'My heart was being ripped out,' he said.
stories.why_it_matters: If you cancel the job that pays 4 dollars and keep the gun that pays two meals, the math is ugly and the child does it.
stories.camps: The White House calls this security first and migration control. Haitian peace workers say drones and task forces without schools and food make more bandits. Gangs already act like the state in places the state left.
